name: Vasuki
notes:
Eleven to fifteen metres, thick through as a man's chest, and no venom at all -- it is a madtsoiid, and it kills by holding. It lies up in the rock shade through the heat and moves at the edges of the day, which is when you find a track across a dune four hand-spans wide and no animal at the end of it.

What it leaves is the skin. A snake this size sheds in one piece and the piece is longer than a boat, lying in the lee of a rock like something discarded rather than something lost. The caravan people do not hunt it and do not need to: they follow the sheds, and a serpent that has shed once will shed again in the same handful of places. Which is why it is recorded as uncommon rather than as a wonder -- the animal is hard to be shown, but the sign of it is all over the rock country if you know the shape of a track.
sources: Vasuki indicus, described from the Kutch lignite 2024
journal_prompt: The track crosses the dune and does not stop, and it is as wide as both my hands laid end to end. I followed it to a rock shelf and found the skin instead of the animal -- whole, from jaw to tail, the eye-caps still in it, and longer than the boat we came down on.
